en: Points of Controversy The Great Fifty The Fifteenth Chapter
The Third Discussion on Perception and Feeling:
Could one who has attained the cessation of perception and feeling die?
Yes, [he could].

Is there, for one who has attained the cessation of perception and feeling, death-related contact, death-related feeling, death-related perception, death-related volition, and death-related consciousness?
One should not say so... [etc. ...

Is it not the case that, for one who has attained the cessation of perception and feeling, there is no death-related contact, no death-related feeling, no death-related perception, no death-related volition, and no death-related consciousness?
“Yes.

“If there is no contact pertaining to death, no feeling pertaining to death, no perception pertaining to death, no volition pertaining to death, and no consciousness pertaining to death for one who has attained the cessation of perception and feeling, then surely it should not be said:
‘One who has attained the cessation of perception and feeling might die.’”
“Could one who has attained the cessation of perception and feeling die?”—
“Yes.”—
“Does one who has attained the cessation of perception and feeling have contact, feeling, perception, volition, and consciousness?”
It should not be said thus … [as before] … Is there no contact,
feeling, perception, volition, or consciousness for one who has attained the cessation of perception and feeling? Yes.
Is it the case that death occurs for one who is without contact, death occurs for one who is without feeling … [and so on] … death occurs for one who is without mind?
One should not say so … Is it not rather the case that death occurs for one who possesses contact … [and so on] … death occurs for one who possesses mind?
“Yes.
“If there is death for one who possesses contact … [and so on] … if there is death for one who possesses mind, then indeed, sir, you should not say:
‘One who has attained the cessation of perception and feeling might die.’”
“Could one who has attained the cessation of perception and feeling die? Yes.
Could poison enter the body of one who has attained the cessation of perception and feeling? Could a weapon enter it? Could fire enter it?”

It should not be said thus … [as before] … “If one has attained the cessation of perception and feeling, would poison not take effect in his body, would a weapon not take effect, and would fire not take effect?
Yes, it would.
If poison would not affect the body of one who has attained the cessation of perception and feeling, and neither a weapon nor fire would affect it, then surely you should not say:
"One who has attained the cessation of perception and feeling might die.
Would one who has attained the cessation of perception and feeling die?
“Yes.
“If that were so, would poison enter the body of one who has attained the cessation of perception and feeling? Would a weapon enter it? Would fire enter it?
“Yes.”
"Has one not attained cessation?
"One should not say so...
[and so on] "...Would one who has attained the cessation of perception and feeling not die?"
“Yes.
“Is there that fixed course by which one who has entered the attainment of the cessation of perception and feeling, being fixed by that fixed course, would not die? “No.”
If there is no such fixed law by which one who has attained the cessation of perception and feeling would not die,
then indeed it should not be said that "one who has attained the cessation of perception and feeling would not die.
[Is it the case that] one possessing eye-consciousness does not die?
“Yes.
“Is there that fixed law by which one who possesses eye-consciousness, being fixed by that law, would not die? “No.”
If there were no such fixed law by which one possessed of eye-consciousness would necessarily not die,
then indeed it should not be said that "one possessed of eye-consciousness does not die.
The Third Discussion on Perception and Feeling is concluded.
